title: CBDT's Fourth Amendment Rules, 2026: A Deep Dive into Tax Recovery, Valuer Registration, and Digital Communication Makeovers
content:
# CBDT's Fourth Amendment Rules, 2026: A Deep Dive into Tax Recovery, Valuer Registration, and Digital Communication Makeovers

In the ever-evolving landscape of Indian taxation, staying updated is not just good practice, it's absolutely crucial. Just when we were getting accustomed to the new **Income-tax Act, 2025**, and the **Income-tax Rules, 2026**, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has dropped another significant update. On September 17, 2026, vide **Notification No. 120/2026**, the CBDT introduced the **Income-tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2026**. This isn't just a routine amendment; it brings about pivotal changes in areas concerning tax recovery procedures, valuer registration, and electronic communication norms.

As tax professionals, we know these amendments aren't merely academic. They directly impact our compliance strategies, the advice we provide, and even the daily grind of our practice. So, chalo, let's break down what these new rules mean for us and our clients.

## Decoding the Key Amendments

The Fourth Amendment Rules, 2026, usher in changes across several critical provisions, some even with retrospective effect. This dual-stage commencement mechanism means some amendments are effective from April 1, 2026, while others kicked in from the notification date itself, September 17, 2026.

### A Major Shift in Tax Recovery: No More Arrests! (Rule 225)

Perhaps the most significant and welcome change is the overhaul of **Rule 225** concerning tax recovery. For years, the specter of arrest and detention loomed large for defaulting taxpayers. But no more! The CBDT has officially removed these provisions as modes of recovery. This move aligns with the government's broader initiative towards decriminalizing technical tax defaults, a step that was also echoed in the Finance Act, 2026.

This is a huge relief, isn't it? It signals a shift in approach, focusing more on property-based recovery rather than personal liberty. While attachment and sale of movable or immovable property, along with the appointment of a receiver, continue to be valid recovery mechanisms, the threat of arrest is now gone from this specific rule.

Interestingly, this amendment to **Rule 225** (and other related rules, 2 to 4 of the Amendment Rules) has been given **retrospective effect from April 1, 2026**.

Let's look at the change:

| Old Provision (Rule 225(4)(c) & Sub-rules 75-83, 91) | New Provision (Effective from April 1, 2026) |
| :------------------------------------------------------ | :-------------------------------------------- |
| Included arrest and detention in prison as a mode of recovery for tax arrears. | **Arrest and detention in prison deleted** as modes of recovery. |
| Detailed procedures for arrest warrant, inquiry, custody, and civil imprisonment. | Corresponding sub-rules (75) to (83) and (91) dealing with arrest and detention have been **omitted**. |

### Streamlining Electronic Communications: Beyond Digital Signatures (Rule 176)

In our increasingly digital world, clear norms for electronic communication are paramount, especially in faceless tax proceedings. The amendment to **Rule 176(3)(a)(ii)** is a step towards making these processes more flexible and technology-neutral. Previously, certain electronic records explicitly required authentication "by affixing digital signature". This has now been replaced with the broader phrase "by way of an electronic communication".

What does this mean in practice? It essentially expands the permissible modes of electronic authentication, moving beyond the sole reliance on digital signatures. This flexibility can certainly make life easier for taxpayers and tax authorities alike in the faceless assessment, verification, and review units.

This particular amendment is effective from the date of publication in the Official Gazette, i.e., **September 17, 2026**.

| Old Provision (Rule 176(3)(a)(ii)) | New Provision (Effective from September 17, 2026) |
| :------------------------------------ | :------------------------------------------------- |
| Required authentication "by affixing digital signature". | Requires authentication "by way of an **electronic communication**". |

### Valuers, Take Note! Revised Registration Norms and Extended Deadlines (Rule 246 & Form 169)

For our colleagues in the valuation fraternity, these amendments bring both revised compliance requirements and a sigh of relief with extended deadlines.

The deadline for individuals who were registered as valuers under the now-repealed **Wealth-tax Act, 1957**, and held a valid certificate as of March 31, 2026, to update their details and continue registration under **Section 514** of the Income-tax Act, 2025, has been extended. The earlier deadline of **September 30, 2026, has now been pushed to March 31, 2027**. A much-needed extension, especially considering the transition to the new Income-tax Act, 2025.

Beyond the date, **Form No. 169**, the application for registration as a Valuer, has been completely substituted. The revised form demands more detailed disclosures, covering personal details, qualifications, professional experience, and declarations concerning potential disqualifications. Also, if you're applying for different classes of assets, you'll need to file separate applications. A fee of ₹10,000 is still applicable, though valuers already registered under the Wealth-tax Act, 1957, get an exemption.

This change, affecting Rule 246 and Form 169, is effective from **September 17, 2026**.

| Old Provision (Rule 246(4)) | New Provision (Effective from September 17, 2026) |
| :------------------------------ | :----------------------------------------------- |
| Deadline to update details for existing valuers: **September 30, 2026**. | Deadline extended to **March 31, 2027**. |

### Relief for Authorised Income-tax Practitioners (AITPs): Extended Timelines (Rule 256 & Form 171)

Similarly, for our dear Authorised Income-tax Practitioners (AITPs), the CBDT has provided an extension. Those registered under the erstwhile Income-tax Act, 1961, and holding valid registration as of March 31, 2026, now have until **March 31, 2027**, to update their details under **Rule 256(4)** and register under **Section 515** of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The previous deadline was also September 30, 2026.

Furthermore, **Form No. 171**, the application for registration as an Authorised Income-tax Practitioner, has been revamped. It now requires comprehensive personal and professional details, including PAN, contact information, principal place of profession, and declarations regarding any disqualifications.

These amendments related to Rule 256 and Form 171 are also effective from **September 17, 2026**.

| Old Provision (Rule 256(4)) | New Provision (Effective from September 17, 2026) |
| :------------------------------ | :----------------------------------------------- |
| Deadline to update details for existing AITPs: **September 30, 2026**. | Deadline extended to **March 31, 2027**. |

### Minor but Important: The Rule 160 Correction

Lastly, a small but necessary technical correction has been made in **Rule 160(3)** and **(4)**, replacing the reference "(i)" with "(a)". These are the kind of clean-up acts that make the rules internally consistent. This change is also retrospective from **April 1, 2026**.

## What's the 'Asli Baat' for Professionals? (The Real Impact)

So, what are the key takeaways for us, the tax and legal professionals?
*   **Decriminalisation is a Trend:** The removal of arrest provisions from tax recovery is a clear signal of the government's intent to move towards a more compliance-friendly regime, de-emphasizing punitive measures for certain defaults. While this is certainly positive, it doesn't mean you can ignore your tax dues! Other stringent recovery mechanisms remain firmly in place.
*   **Digitalisation is Deepening:** The shift to "electronic communication" from "digital signature" in **Rule 176** shows a pragmatic approach to digital interactions. It acknowledges the diverse ways electronic authentication can occur, providing flexibility in faceless proceedings. We must ensure our systems and client communication methods are aligned with this broader definition.
*   **Time to Act for Valuers and AITPs:** The extended deadlines for registration for both valuers and Authorised Income-tax Practitioners are a welcome relief, giving them more time to transition into the new framework. However, this extension should not lead to complacency. The revised forms (Form 169 and 171) demand comprehensive details, so it's advisable to prepare and submit these applications well in advance of the new March 31, 2027, deadline. For valuers, particularly, the enhanced disclosure requirements in Form 169 underscore the increased scrutiny and professionalism expected.
*   **Understanding the New Framework:** With the Income-tax Act, 2025, and Income-tax Rules, 2026, now fully in play (replacing the 1961 Act and 1962 Rules), these continuous amendments are part of the ongoing refinement. It's imperative to always refer to the latest rules and forms, as the old ones are no longer applicable. *Yeh purane rules ab applicable nahi hain, bhai!*

## Conclusion

The Income-tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2026, are a testament to the dynamic nature of our tax laws. From ushering in a more humane approach to tax recovery to streamlining digital interactions and providing much-needed extensions for professional registrations, these amendments are critical. As professionals, our role is to not just understand these changes but to effectively communicate and implement them, ensuring our clients remain compliant in this ever-evolving tax ecosystem. So, let's keep learning, keep adapting, and keep advising with precision!
